timeline.name: Treaty of Amritsar creates the Dogra state of Jammu and Kashmir
timeline.line: British sell the Kashmir valley to Gulab Singh, assembling the princely state later disputed
timeline.description: After the First Anglo-Sikh War the East India Company transferred Kashmir to Gulab Singh for a cash payment, joining it to Jammu under Dogra rule. A Hindu dynasty came to rule a Muslim-majority valley.
timeline.immediate_effect: A composite princely state under British paramountcy.
timeline.long_term_effect: Its external boundaries define what India and Pakistan dispute today; its ruler-population religious mismatch shaped 1947.

timeline.name: Muslim League's Lahore Resolution
timeline.line: Muslim League demands independent states for Muslim-majority areas
timeline.description: The All-India Muslim League called for 'independent states' in Muslim-majority regions of the north-west and east. Pakistan marks 23 March as Pakistan Day.
timeline.immediate_effect: Partition became the League's stated goal.
timeline.long_term_effect: The founding text of the two-nation idea that Pakistani leaders still invoke about Kashmir.

timeline.name: Partition and independence of India and Pakistan
timeline.line: British India partitioned into India and Pakistan amid mass killing and migration
timeline.description: The Indian Independence Act created two dominions from 15 August 1947; the Radcliffe boundaries were published only on 17 August. Communal violence and migration followed; estimates of deaths range from about 200,000 to two million and of displaced people from 10 to 20 million.
timeline.immediate_effect: Two hostile successor states; Pakistan in two wings 1,600 km apart; princely states left to accede.
timeline.long_term_effect: Kashmir's unresolved accession, divided Punjab canal systems, and a founding memory of violence both states commemorate.

timeline.name: First India-Pakistan War (Kashmir)
timeline.line: First war splits Kashmir along a ceasefire line that still divides it
timeline.description: Tribal forces from Pakistan's North-West Frontier entered the state in October 1947; Indian troops arrived after the accession and Pakistani regulars joined in 1948. A UN-brokered ceasefire took effect on 1 January 1949.
timeline.immediate_effect: India held about two-thirds of the state including the valley; Pakistan held Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan.
timeline.long_term_effect: The ceasefire line became the 1972 Line of Control, the de facto border.

timeline.name: Tribal lashkar invasion of Jammu and Kashmir
timeline.line: Pashtun tribal forces cross into Kashmir, triggering accession and war
timeline.description: Tribal fighters entered via Muzaffarabad and sacked Baramulla before Indian forces halted them near Srinagar. Indian accounts describe Pakistani official organization; Pakistani accounts describe a spontaneous response to attacks on Muslims in Jammu. Pakistani regulars entered openly in 1948.
timeline.immediate_effect: Accession to India and full war.
timeline.long_term_effect: Division of the state.

timeline.name: Maharaja Hari Singh accedes to India
timeline.line: Facing a tribal invasion, Kashmir's ruler signs accession to India; Indian troops fly in
timeline.description: With tribal forces advancing on Srinagar, the Maharaja signed the Instrument of Accession and Indian troops were airlifted on 27 October. Mountbatten's acceptance said the question should be settled by reference to the people once order was restored. Whether the instrument was signed before or after troops landed, and its validity, are disputed between Indian and Pakistani accounts.
timeline.immediate_effect: First India-Pakistan war in Kashmir.
timeline.long_term_effect: India's legal claim rests on the accession; Pakistan's case rests on the plebiscite promise and the Muslim-majority population.

timeline.name: UN Security Council resolutions on Kashmir and the plebiscite
timeline.line: UN calls for a plebiscite after withdrawals; the sequencing is never agreed
timeline.description: India referred the conflict to the Security Council on 1 January 1948. Resolution 39 created UNCIP and Resolution 47 set out steps toward a plebiscite; UNCIP's August 1948 resolution required Pakistani withdrawal first. The two sides never agreed on demilitarization, so no plebiscite was held.
timeline.immediate_effect: Ceasefire from 1 January 1949 and UN observers.
timeline.long_term_effect: Pakistan still cites the resolutions; India argues Pakistan's failure to withdraw and the Simla Agreement superseded them.

timeline.name: Karachi Agreement (ceasefire line in Jammu and Kashmir)
timeline.line: Military representatives draw the ceasefire line across Kashmir, stopping at NJ9842
timeline.description: Defined the ceasefire line to be supervised by UN military observers; it ended at map point NJ9842 and described the area beyond only as running 'thence north to the glaciers'.
timeline.problem_solved: Stabilized the 1949 ceasefire.
timeline.did_it_survive: Partly: superseded in India's view by the 1972 LoC, which follows it closely; its undefined northern end produced the Siachen conflict.

timeline.name: US-Pakistan Mutual Defense Assistance Agreement (with SEATO 1954 and the Baghdad Pact/CENTO 1955)
timeline.line: Pakistan joins the US Cold War alliance system
timeline.description: Brought US arms to Pakistan; Pakistan joined SEATO (1954) and the Baghdad Pact (1955, later CENTO). The alliances were aimed at communism; Pakistan hoped they would help against India.
timeline.problem_solved: For the US, containment on the Soviet and Chinese periphery; for Pakistan, arms against a larger India.
timeline.did_it_survive: No: the US cut arms in 1965 and did not fight for Pakistan in 1971; Pakistan left SEATO in 1972-73 and CENTO in 1979. Cooperation revived without a treaty in the 1980s and after 2001.

timeline.name: Indus Waters Treaty
timeline.line: World Bank-brokered treaty divides the Indus rivers between India and Pakistan
timeline.description: Allocated the eastern rivers to India and the western rivers to Pakistan, created the Permanent Indus Commission and a three-tier dispute process, with the World Bank as a signatory for specific functions.
timeline.problem_solved: The canal-water conflict created by partition, including India's April 1948 stoppage of flows.
timeline.did_it_survive: Survived the 1965, 1971 and 1999 wars; India has held it in abeyance since April 2025, a status Pakistan and the treaty's text do not provide for (contested).

timeline.name: Sino-Indian War
timeline.line: China defeats India in the Himalayas, opening the door to Sino-Pakistani alignment
timeline.description: A month-long war in Ladakh and the North-East Frontier ended with a Chinese unilateral ceasefire and China holding Aksai Chin.
timeline.immediate_effect: Indian rearmament with Western and Soviet help.
timeline.long_term_effect: China and Pakistan aligned against a common rival within months (1963 boundary agreement); India plans for a two-front threat.

timeline.name: China-Pakistan Boundary Agreement
timeline.line: Pakistan and China settle the Gilgit-Baltistan-Xinjiang boundary; Shaksgam goes to China
timeline.description: Delimited the boundary between Xinjiang and Pakistani-held territory; Article 6 makes it provisional pending a Kashmir settlement, after which the sovereign authority is to reopen negotiations.
timeline.problem_solved: Removed a China-Pakistan border quarrel and built an alignment against India.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, in force; India rejects it.

timeline.name: Operation Gibraltar
timeline.line: Pakistani infiltrators try to ignite a Kashmir uprising; locals do not rise
timeline.description: Several thousand Pakistani-trained infiltrators crossed the ceasefire line; the expected revolt did not occur, and Pakistan followed with a conventional thrust (Grand Slam) that led to general war.
timeline.immediate_effect: India crossed the international border on 6 September.
timeline.long_term_effect: The failure of an assumed popular uprising is a warning about planning on local support.

timeline.name: Second India-Pakistan War
timeline.line: Pakistan's Kashmir infiltration fails; India counters across the Punjab border; stalemate
timeline.description: Pakistan's attempt to spark a Kashmir uprising (August) and its thrust toward Akhnoor (1 September) led India to attack across the international border toward Lahore on 6 September. The US and UK cut arms to both; the war ended in a UN ceasefire and Soviet-mediated Tashkent talks.
timeline.immediate_effect: Return to pre-war lines; both sides claim success.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed that India would widen a Kashmir fight to the international border; pushed Pakistan toward China after the US arms cutoff.

timeline.name: Tashkent Declaration
timeline.line: Soviet-mediated deal returns both armies to pre-war positions
timeline.description: Shastri and Ayub Khan agreed to withdraw to positions held before 5 August 1965 and to settle disputes peacefully; it did not address Kashmir's status.
timeline.problem_solved: Ending the 1965 war.
timeline.did_it_survive: Withdrawals were implemented; its non-use-of-force pledge failed in 1971.

timeline.name: Rann of Kutch arbitration agreement and award
timeline.line: After April 1965 clashes, a UK-brokered deal sends the Kutch boundary to binding arbitration
timeline.description: A June 1965 agreement mediated by the British government referred the western boundary to a tribunal, whose February 1968 award gave Pakistan about a tenth of its claim; both implemented it.
timeline.problem_solved: A live border clash in the Rann.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes: the only India-Pakistan land boundary settled by arbitration; Sir Creek was left unresolved.

timeline.name: Pakistan's crackdown in East Pakistan and the birth of Bangladesh
timeline.line: Army crackdown on East Pakistan after the Awami League's election win; Bangladesh declares independence
timeline.description: After the Awami League won a national majority in the December 1970 election and power was not transferred, the army began Operation Searchlight on 25 March 1971. Roughly 10 million refugees fled to India; the death toll is disputed, with estimates from about 300,000 to 3 million.
timeline.immediate_effect: Indian support to Bengali insurgents and a refugee burden that framed India's case for war.
timeline.long_term_effect: Pakistan lost half its population in December 1971; the loss drives Pakistani fears of Indian dismemberment.

timeline.name: Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation
timeline.line: India signs a 20-year treaty with Moscow months before the Bangladesh war
timeline.description: Article IX provided for immediate mutual consultations if either was attacked or threatened. Not a mutual defence pact, but it deterred Chinese and US intervention in 1971.
timeline.problem_solved: Insurance against China and the US before intervening in East Pakistan.
timeline.did_it_survive: Ran its 20-year term; replaced by the 1993 Indo-Russian friendship treaty without the security clause; the arms relationship continues.

timeline.name: Third India-Pakistan War (Bangladesh Liberation War)
timeline.line: India's intervention ends with Pakistan's surrender in Dhaka and an independent Bangladesh
timeline.description: After Pakistani air strikes on Indian bases on 3 December, India attacked in the east alongside Bengali forces; Pakistani forces in Dhaka surrendered on 16 December and about 93,000 personnel became prisoners. The US sent a carrier group to the Bay of Bengal; the Indo-Soviet treaty deterred wider intervention.
timeline.immediate_effect: Bangladesh independent; India held Pakistani prisoners and territory in the west.
timeline.long_term_effect: Settled conventional superiority in India's favour and drove Pakistan's nuclear program; led to the Simla Agreement.

timeline.name: Pakistan launches its nuclear weapons effort after 1971
timeline.line: Bhutto convenes scientists after the 1971 defeat and starts the drive for a bomb
timeline.description: Accounts describe a January 1972 meeting in Multan where Zulfikar Ali Bhutto asked Pakistani scientists to build a nuclear weapon; India's 1974 test accelerated the program. The meeting is documented in secondary histories rather than a public record.
timeline.immediate_effect: A secret enrichment and weapons program.
timeline.long_term_effect: Nuclear weapons became Pakistan's answer to conventional inferiority revealed in 1971.

timeline.name: Simla Agreement
timeline.line: Simla Agreement converts the ceasefire line into the Line of Control and commits both to bilateral settlement
timeline.description: Committed both to settle differences 'by peaceful means through bilateral negotiations or by any other peaceful means mutually agreed' and made the line resulting from the 17 December 1971 ceasefire a Line of Control that neither side would seek to alter unilaterally.
timeline.problem_solved: Post-1971 withdrawals and a framework to return prisoners.
timeline.did_it_survive: Formally in force, but contested: India reads it as ruling out third-party roles; Pakistan says it does not supersede UN resolutions and in April 2025 threatened to hold it in abeyance. Kargil (1999) violated its LoC clause.

timeline.name: India's first nuclear test ('Smiling Buddha')
timeline.line: India tests a 'peaceful nuclear explosion' at Pokhran
timeline.description: India described the test as a peaceful nuclear explosion; it did not declare weapons status until 1998.
timeline.immediate_effect: Creation of the Nuclear Suppliers Group and export controls against India.
timeline.long_term_effect: Accelerated Pakistan's program and began the nuclear rivalry.

timeline.name: Operation Meghdoot: India occupies the Siachen glacier
timeline.line: India pre-empts Pakistan onto the Saltoro Ridge; two decades of high-altitude fighting follow
timeline.description: Indian troops occupied the Saltoro Ridge passes in April 1984 in an area the 1949 and 1972 lines left undefined; Pakistan's attempts to dislodge them failed. Firing largely stopped with the 2003 ceasefire; demilitarization talks have not succeeded.
timeline.immediate_effect: Indian control of the glacier.
timeline.long_term_effect: A frozen, costly deployment and an unresolved line.

timeline.name: Exercise Brasstacks crisis
timeline.line: India's giant Rajasthan exercise prompts Pakistani counter-deployments and a war scare
timeline.description: A very large Indian exercise near the border and Pakistani deployments opposite Punjab produced a standoff defused by a February 1987 agreement to pull back. Whether Pakistan sent a deliberate nuclear signal (an A.Q. Khan interview published in March 1987) and whether India intended provocation are contested.
timeline.immediate_effect: Mutual pullback.
timeline.long_term_effect: Contributed to the 1988 nuclear-installations agreement and the 1991 exercise-notification agreement.

timeline.name: Agreement on the Prohibition of Attack against Nuclear Installations
timeline.line: India and Pakistan agree not to attack each other's nuclear facilities
timeline.description: Each side refrains from attacking the other's listed nuclear installations and exchanges lists every 1 January.
timeline.problem_solved: Fear of pre-emptive strikes on nuclear facilities during the 1980s.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes: lists have been exchanged annually since 1992, including in crisis years.

timeline.name: Armed insurgency begins in the Kashmir valley
timeline.line: Insurgency erupts in Kashmir after the disputed 1987 state election
timeline.description: Militancy grew after the contested 1987 state election and escalated from late 1989; most Kashmiri Pandits fled the valley in early 1990. India attributes the insurgency to Pakistani training, arms and infiltration; Pakistan describes an indigenous uprising it supports politically. Both elements are documented and their weight is contested.
timeline.immediate_effect: Large Indian counter-insurgency deployment; the 1990 crisis.
timeline.long_term_effect: Terror attacks by Pakistan-based groups replaced conventional war as the main trigger of India-Pakistan crises.

timeline.name: 1990 Kashmir crisis
timeline.line: Troop movements and insurgency push both sides to a war scare; a US envoy visits
timeline.description: As the Kashmir insurgency surged, deployments and rhetoric raised fears of war; US Deputy NSA Robert Gates visited both capitals in May 1990 and tensions eased. Claims that Pakistan readied nuclear weapons are disputed, and some participants judge the danger was overstated.
timeline.immediate_effect: De-escalation and new confidence-building measures.
timeline.long_term_effect: First instance of US crisis diplomacy in the nuclear-shadow era.

timeline.name: US cuts aid to Pakistan under the Pressler Amendment
timeline.line: With the Afghan war over, Washington stops certifying Pakistan is bomb-free and cuts aid
timeline.description: The Pressler Amendment required annual certification that Pakistan did not possess a nuclear explosive device; President Bush declined in 1990, halting most aid and F-16 deliveries.
timeline.immediate_effect: Pakistan's arms dependence shifted further toward China.
timeline.long_term_effect: Pakistan's memory of US abandonment after Afghanistan is a recurring theme in its view of Washington.

timeline.name: India and Pakistan test nuclear weapons
timeline.line: India tests at Pokhran; Pakistan answers at Chagai: an overt nuclear dyad
timeline.description: India tested on 11 and 13 May and Pakistan on 28 and 30 May 1998. Security Council Resolution 1172 condemned both and demanded restraint; the US imposed sanctions.
timeline.immediate_effect: Sanctions on both; the Lahore summit followed within a year.
timeline.long_term_effect: Every later crisis has been fought under nuclear deterrence, capping war aims and inviting outside crisis management.

timeline.name: Lahore Declaration and MOU
timeline.line: Vajpayee rides the bus to Lahore; the new nuclear powers pledge to avoid conflict
timeline.description: The declaration recognized that the nuclear dimension added to their responsibility to avoid conflict; the MOU promised nuclear confidence-building measures including advance notice of missile tests.
timeline.problem_solved: Post-1998 nuclear risk.
timeline.did_it_survive: Politically broken within months by Kargil; its missile pre-notification idea was realized in the 2005 agreement.

timeline.name: Kargil War
timeline.line: First war between nuclear-armed neighbours: Pakistani troops seize Kargil heights and are pushed back
timeline.description: Pakistani Northern Light Infantry soldiers, initially presented as mujahideen, occupied heights on the Indian side of the LoC vacated over winter. India retook most positions without crossing the LoC; under US pressure Sharif agreed at Blair House on 4 July to withdraw. India's official toll was 527 dead; Pakistani figures are disputed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Restoration of the LoC; Pakistani civil-military crisis leading to the October coup.
timeline.long_term_effect: Became the central case for the stability-instability paradox and for US crisis management in South Asia.

timeline.name: Kargil heights seizure
timeline.line: Disguised Pakistani regulars seize LoC heights; India fights back without crossing the line
timeline.description: The only case in the class under overt nuclear deterrence. India kept operations on its side of the LoC, the US pressed Pakistan to withdraw, and the fighting stayed local.
timeline.immediate_effect: Pakistani withdrawal.
timeline.long_term_effect: Indian restraint (no LoC crossing) became the benchmark later governments moved away from.

timeline.name: Musharraf overthrows Nawaz Sharif
timeline.line: Army chief Musharraf seizes power three months after Kargil
timeline.description: After Sharif tried to dismiss him, Musharraf took power in a bloodless coup; the Kargil withdrawal was a source of the civil-military rupture.
timeline.immediate_effect: Military rule until 2008.
timeline.long_term_effect: Reinforced the army's control over India policy under later civilian governments.

timeline.name: India's Operation Parakram
timeline.description: Ten-month full mobilization after the attack on India's parliament; no war under nuclear shadow; stood down in October 2002.

timeline.name: Musharraf's pledge on terrorism and the composite dialogue
timeline.line: Pakistan pledges its territory will not be used for terrorism; peace process begins
timeline.description: Following the November 2003 LoC ceasefire, the joint statement recorded Musharraf's assurance that Pakistani-controlled territory would not be used to support terrorism, and both sides launched a composite dialogue.
timeline.immediate_effect: The most sustained peace process (2004-2008), with reduced infiltration and violence.
timeline.long_term_effect: India measures Pakistan against this pledge; the 2008 Mumbai attacks ended the process.

timeline.name: Agreement on Pre-Notification of Flight Testing of Ballistic Missiles
timeline.line: Both sides agree to notify each other before ballistic missile tests
timeline.description: Requires advance notification of surface-to-surface ballistic missile flight tests; cruise missiles are not covered.
timeline.problem_solved: Risk that a test is mistaken for an attack.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, formally in force; the 2022 BrahMos accident involved a cruise missile outside its scope.

timeline.name: Nuclear Suppliers Group waiver for India
timeline.line: US-backed waiver lets India trade in civil nuclear technology; Pakistan is refused the same
timeline.description: Following the US-India civil nuclear initiative, the NSG exempted India from its full-scope safeguards requirement.
timeline.immediate_effect: Pakistan protested discrimination and sought a similar deal from China.
timeline.long_term_effect: Symbolizes the US tilt toward India as a strategic partner.

timeline.name: Mumbai attacks crisis
timeline.line: Lashkar gunmen kill 166 in Mumbai; India chooses diplomacy over strikes
timeline.description: Ten attackers who came by sea killed 166 people over three days; the surviving gunman was tried and convicted in India. Pakistan's government acknowledged in February 2009 that part of the plot was carried out from Pakistan, but prosecutions there stalled. India suspended the peace process and did not use force.
timeline.immediate_effect: End of the composite dialogue; international pressure on Pakistan.
timeline.long_term_effect: Indian political consensus that non-military responses had failed shaped later governments' choices.

timeline.name: China-Pakistan Economic Corridor launched
timeline.line: Xi visits Islamabad and launches CPEC through Gilgit-Baltistan
timeline.description: During Xi Jinping's April 2015 visit the two governments upgraded ties to an 'all-weather strategic cooperative partnership' and launched the corridor, routed through Pakistani-administered Kashmir. India objects that it violates its sovereignty.
timeline.immediate_effect: Large Chinese financing of Pakistani power and roads.
timeline.long_term_effect: Gives China a material stake in Pakistan's stability and in the Kashmir status quo.

timeline.name: Pathankot air base attack
timeline.line: Militants attack an Indian air base a week after Modi's Lahore visit; India tries a joint investigation
timeline.description: Attackers India linked to JeM killed seven security personnel at Pathankot. India allowed a Pakistani joint investigation team to visit; the process collapsed with mutual recrimination.
timeline.immediate_effect: Planned talks postponed; no military action.
timeline.long_term_effect: The failed cooperative track preceded India's shift to military responses after Uri.

timeline.name: Uri attack and cross-LoC 'surgical strikes'
timeline.line: After Uri, India publicly announces raids across the LoC; Pakistan denies they happened
timeline.description: An attack on an army camp at Uri killed 19 soldiers. On 29 September India's DGMO announced strikes on 'launch pads' across the LoC; Pakistan's military denied any strikes and reported only cross-border firing, which gave it room not to retaliate.
timeline.immediate_effect: No escalation beyond LoC firing.
timeline.long_term_effect: India broke its taboo on publicly acknowledged cross-LoC action.

timeline.name: Pulwama bombing and Balakot air strikes
timeline.line: India bombs Balakot after Pulwama; Pakistan strikes back and returns a captured pilot
timeline.description: A JeM-claimed suicide bombing killed 40 Indian paramilitary personnel. On 26 February Indian jets struck at Balakot in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; Pakistan retaliated with air strikes on 27 February and shot down an Indian MiG-21, releasing the pilot on 1 March. Damage at Balakot and India's claim to have downed a Pakistani F-16 are both disputed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Crisis ended within two weeks; both sides claimed victory.
timeline.long_term_effect: First air strikes across the international border since 1971 between nuclear powers without further escalation; both publics saw their side as having won.

timeline.name: India revokes Jammu and Kashmir's special status
timeline.line: India ends Article 370 autonomy and splits the state into two union territories
timeline.description: A presidential order and the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act ended the state's special status and created the union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh from 31 October 2019, under a lockdown and communications blackout. Pakistan downgraded diplomatic relations and suspended trade; India's Supreme Court upheld the change in December 2023.
timeline.immediate_effect: Diplomatic downgrade and trade suspension; Chinese objection over Ladakh.
timeline.long_term_effect: Removed the constitutional ambiguity India had kept since 1949; Pakistan marks 5 August annually as a day of protest.

timeline.name: Galwan valley clash with China
timeline.line: First deadly India-China clash in 45 years brings the two-front problem back
timeline.description: Twenty Indian soldiers and at least four Chinese soldiers (China's acknowledged figure) died in hand-to-hand fighting in Ladakh.
timeline.immediate_effect: Large Indian redeployment to the China front.
timeline.long_term_effect: India's Pakistan planning must account for China tying down forces in Ladakh.

timeline.name: DGMOs recommit to the 2003 LoC ceasefire
timeline.line: Army hotline deal sharply cuts LoC firing after years of violations
timeline.description: A joint statement by the directors general of military operations recommitted both armies to all agreements and understandings on the LoC. Firing fell steeply afterwards.
timeline.immediate_effect: Quieter LoC through 2021-2024.
timeline.long_term_effect: Shows the military hotline can deliver restraint without a political process; it did not survive the 2025 fighting intact.

timeline.name: Indian BrahMos missile accidentally lands in Pakistan
timeline.line: An Indian cruise missile fired by accident lands near Mian Channu; neither side escalates
timeline.description: India said a routine maintenance error caused the launch and later dismissed three officers; Pakistan protested that it received no hotline warning.
timeline.immediate_effect: No retaliation; diplomatic protest.
timeline.long_term_effect: Evidence both of restraint in peacetime and of thin crisis-communication channels between nuclear-armed neighbours.

timeline.name: India seeks to modify the Indus Waters Treaty; arbitration proceeds without India
timeline.line: India issues notice to modify the water treaty as parallel dispute processes run
timeline.description: After the World Bank activated both a Neutral Expert (India's choice) and a Court of Arbitration (Pakistan's choice) over the Kishenganga and Ratle projects, India gave notice under Article XII(3). The Court ruled it had competence in 2023; India does not participate.
timeline.immediate_effect: Treaty dispute machinery split along national preferences.
timeline.long_term_effect: Prefigured the 2025 decision to hold the treaty in abeyance.

timeline.name: Pahalgam attack and Operation Sindoor
timeline.line: India strikes deep into Pakistan after the Pahalgam massacre; four days of missile and drone war end in a ceasefire
timeline.description: Gunmen killed 26 people, mostly tourists, at Pahalgam on 22 April. On 7 May India struck nine sites it called terrorist infrastructure, including in Bahawalpur and Muridke; after drone and artillery exchanges, both sides struck military targets including Pakistani air bases on 10 May, and a ceasefire took effect that evening. The US announced the ceasefire and Pakistan credited US mediation; India says it was agreed bilaterally between DGMOs. Aircraft losses were acknowledged only in part by India and disputed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Ceasefire holding; trade, visas, airspace and the water treaty remained suspended.
timeline.long_term_effect: Set the deepest post-1971 precedent for strikes on each other's heartland under nuclear deterrence, and India declared the response template official policy.

timeline.name: India holds the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance
timeline.line: After Pahalgam, India suspends its participation in the treaty that survived three wars
timeline.description: India's Cabinet Committee on Security put the treaty 'in abeyance' until Pakistan 'credibly and irrevocably abjures' support for cross-border terrorism, and cut visas, defence attaches and mission strength. Pakistan's National Security Committee said any diversion of its water would be treated as an act of war and that it could hold bilateral agreements including Simla in abeyance. The treaty has no unilateral suspension clause; whether abeyance is lawful is contested, and the Court of Arbitration held in June 2025 that it did not affect its competence.
timeline.immediate_effect: India stopped data sharing and Indus Commission meetings.
timeline.long_term_effect: Water is now an explicit coercive lever in the rivalry; no treaty framework currently governs the Indus in practice.

timeline.name: Pakistan-Saudi Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement signed
timeline.line: Pakistan and Saudi Arabia agree that aggression against one is aggression against both
timeline.description: Signed in Riyadh four months after the May 2025 fighting, the agreement states that aggression against either is aggression against both. Its text beyond the joint statement is not public, and whether it covers India scenarios or nuclear guarantees is unstated.
timeline.immediate_effect: India said it would study the implications for its security.
timeline.long_term_effect: First formal mutual defence commitment Pakistan has held since leaving CENTO in 1979; its operational meaning is untested.

timeline.name: Pakistan-Saudi Arabia Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement
timeline.line: Mutual defence pact: aggression against one is aggression against both
timeline.description: Formalizes decades of Pakistani military presence and training in Saudi Arabia and Saudi financial support into a mutual defence commitment.
timeline.problem_solved: For Riyadh, a hedge on US guarantees; for Islamabad, finance and a partner after the May 2025 crisis (assessed motives, not stated text).
timeline.did_it_survive: Untested as of its signing.

timeline.name: Pakistan's 27th Amendment creates a Chief of Defence Forces
timeline.line: Constitutional change places the armed forces under a single army-led chief
timeline.description: The amendment created the post of Chief of Defence Forces, held by the army chief, and a Federal Constitutional Court. Details of command over strategic forces are reported rather than fully public.
timeline.immediate_effect: Field Marshal Munir's authority formalized.
timeline.long_term_effect: Concentrates crisis decision-making, including over nuclear-capable forces, in the army leadership.

territories.name: Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh (Indian-administered)

current_claims.basis: 1947 Instrument of Accession; Indian Parliament's 1994 resolution claims the entire former princely state
disputed territory whose status must be settled by the plebiscite in UNSC resolutions; Pakistan's 2020 official map shows all of it as disputed/Pakistani

territories.recognition: No general international recognition of either side's full claim. The UN treats Kashmir as disputed (UNMOGIP still deployed); India holds the dispute is bilateral under Simla and that the 2019 reorganization is an internal matter.
significance: national-identity (secular India vs. two-nation theory)
water (headwaters of the Jhelum and Chenab)
military (LoC, Siachen access)

territories.name: Azad Jammu and Kashmir

lessons.name: India: no first use, massive retaliation
lessons.description: India's 2003 CCS statement declares no first use, retaliation 'massive and designed to inflict unacceptable damage', and an exception allowing a nuclear response to major biological or chemical attack. Periodic official remarks that NFU could change do not amend the published doctrine.

lessons.name: India: terror attacks will be answered militarily; 'nuclear blackmail' will not deter
lessons.description: In his 12 May 2025 address the Prime Minister stated that India would respond to terror attacks on its own terms, would not tolerate nuclear blackmail, and would not distinguish sponsoring governments from terrorists. This is declared policy in a speech, not a published doctrine document, and it narrows future leaders' room to choose restraint.

lessons.name: Pakistan: nuclear weapons offset conventional inferiority, with no first-use pledge
lessons.description: Pakistan has published no nuclear doctrine, refuses a no-first-use pledge and describes its posture in official statements as 'credible minimum' and later 'full spectrum' deterrence. The literature reads this as a lesson of 1971: first-use ambiguity is meant to deter Indian conventional offensives. The link to 1971 is interpretation, not a Pakistani document.

lessons.name: Nuclear deterrence has permitted limited violence below the war threshold
lessons.description: Kargil and the post-2016 strike rounds are widely cited as the stability-instability paradox: neither side fears total war, so both take limited risks. Scholars disagree on the mechanism; Kapur argues nuclear weapons made Pakistan more risk-acceptant, while others credit deterrence with keeping every crisis short. Both readings fit the same cases.

lessons.name: Outside powers, mainly the US, have helped end nuclear-era crises
lessons.description: The literature credits US diplomacy with ending or easing the 1990, 1999 and 2001-02 crises. In 2019 and 2025 the US role is disputed: Pakistan credits it, India publicly denies mediation. Rising Indian resistance to third parties may make this channel less reliable in future.

lessons.name: Deniable offensives in Kashmir have escalated beyond Pakistan's plan
lessons.description: In 1947, 1965 and 1999 an operation that began with irregulars or disguised troops drew in regular forces, widened the war or forced a humiliating withdrawal. This pattern is an inference from three cases, not Pakistani doctrine, and differences in context between them are large.

lessons.name: India answers pressure in Kashmir by choosing a different theatre or lever
lessons.description: In 1965 India crossed the Punjab border rather than fight only in Kashmir; in 1971 it acted in the east; since 2019 it has struck outside Kashmir and used trade and water. The unifying reading is an analyst inference; Kargil, where India deliberately did not cross the LoC, is the main counter-example.

tendencies.name: India's military responses to major attacks have become more overt and deeper each round since 2016
current_evidence: The May 2025 address declared military response the standing policy, and trade, visas and the water treaty remained suspended after the ceasefire.
tendencies.caveat: All three supporting cases are under one prime minister; the contradicting cases include restraint under earlier governments and early in Modi's own tenure. Each round also ended within days, so the trend is in the depth of the opening strike, not in willingness to fight a long war.

tendencies.name: Pakistan answers overt Indian strikes with a visible counter-strike within days, then accepts a halt
current_evidence: In May 2025 the counter-operation came within about three days and a ceasefire was agreed the same day.
tendencies.caveat: In 2016 Pakistan denied the Indian strikes happened and so avoided retaliating; in 1999 it withdrew rather than widen the war. n is two for the pattern, and a strike the army cannot deny appears to be the condition for retaliation.

tendencies.name: Pakistan's security establishment has used non-state or disguised forces to press on Kashmir
current_evidence: India attributes the 2025 Pahalgam attack to an LeT proxy and the US designated TRF a terrorist organization; Pakistan denies involvement and offered a neutral investigation.
tendencies.caveat: State involvement is admitted for 1965 and documented for 1999 but denied for recent attacks, where evidence is mostly Indian and US statements. Infiltration and violence fell sharply in 2004-2008 and 2021-2024, so the tendency depends on Pakistani leadership choices and external pressure rather than being constant.

path_dependencies.name: From the 1846 princely state to today's Line of Control

chain.step: 1846 treaty assembles a Muslim-majority state under a Hindu ruler
1947 invasion and contested accession to India
UN plebiscite plan stalls over withdrawal sequencing; 1949 ceasefire line
1972 Simla makes it the Line of Control and India reads the dispute as bilateral
Undefined northern end produces Siachen; insurgency from 1989
2019 India removes Article 370; Pakistan downgrades ties
Current constraint: a de facto partition neither side accepts de jure, with China holding a third share

path_dependencies.description: The documents at each step exist; the causal weight given to each arrow is an assessment, and alternatives (e.g. that the 1987 election mattered more than any treaty for the insurgency) are plausible.

path_dependencies.name: From the 1971 defeat to limited wars under nuclear deterrence

chain.step: 1971 loss of East Pakistan shows Pakistan's conventional inferiority
Pakistan starts a weapons program; India tests in 1974
1998 overt tests
Kargil tests whether limited action is safe under the nuclear umbrella
India develops stand-off options below Pakistan's presumed thresholds
Current constraint: short, sharp exchanges on heartland targets with each side assuming the other will stop first

path_dependencies.description: Arrows are hypotheses. Pakistan's program also drew on India's own program and on regional prestige; the claim that deterrence caused rather than merely coincided with short crises is contested (see lesson:stability_instability).

path_dependencies.name: From partition's canal split to water as a coercive lever

chain.step: 1947 boundary leaves Pakistani canals fed from headworks in India
1960 treaty divides the rivers and survives three wars
2016-2023 project disputes split the treaty's dispute machinery; India seeks modification
2025 India holds the treaty in abeyance; Pakistan calls diversion an act of war
Current constraint: India's physical ability to cut flows is limited in the short run, so the lever is data, timing and future dams

path_dependencies.description: Each step is documented; whether 2025 is a durable end of treaty cooperation or a bargaining position is an open question.

narratives.name: Pakistan: Kashmir as the 'jugular vein' and unfinished business of partition
narratives.historical_event: The 1940 Lahore Resolution, the Muslim-majority state's 1947 accession to India, and the unfulfilled UN plebiscite.
narratives.modern_interpretation: Pakistani leaders present Kashmir as the incomplete part of the two-nation project and India's rule as occupation. The army chief used the 'jugular vein' phrase and two-nation framing in April 2025; the state marks 5 February and 5 August annually. The attribution of the 'jugular vein' phrase to Jinnah is itself debated.

narratives.name: India: Jammu and Kashmir, including Pakistani-held areas, is an integral part of India
narratives.historical_event: The 1947 Instrument of Accession and the 1994 parliamentary resolution.
narratives.modern_interpretation: Indian governments treat the accession as final and the only remaining issue as Pakistan's 'illegal occupation'. The 2019 abrogation was presented as completing integration, and India refuses third-party roles citing Simla. The accession is a documented event; the claim that it closed the question is a political position Pakistan and the UN record do not share.
used_in: PM's 12 May 2025 address (talks only on terrorism and PoK)

narratives.name: Partition as a founding trauma, commemorated separately
narratives.modern_interpretation: India declared 14 August 'Partition Horrors Remembrance Day' in 2021, the day Pakistan celebrates independence; Pakistani commemoration emphasizes the sacrifice of Muslim migrants and Hindu-Sikh violence. Each state's memory places blame differently.
used_in: Independence Day speeches in both countries

narratives.name: 1971: India's victory, Pakistan's dismemberment
narratives.historical_event: The December 1971 war and the Dhaka surrender.
narratives.modern_interpretation: India commemorates 16 December as Vijay Diwas; in Pakistan the loss is framed as Indian-engineered dismemberment, a memory invoked to explain nuclear deterrence and, after May 2025, official claims to have restored deterrence. The scale of the 1971 killings and responsibility remain contested among all three states.
used_in: Pakistani official commentary on the May 2025 fighting

cases.name: Egyptian and Syrian mobilization under exercise cover, October 1973
Iraqi buildup on the Kuwaiti border, July 1990
Seizure of Crimea and outbreak of the Donbas war
Russian spring 2021 buildup on Ukraine's border

border_mobilization.selection_note: Cases are large, visible troop concentrations on a neighbour's border. The set is drawn from well-documented crises and is biased toward mobilizations that became famous because they led to war; quiet buildups that dissolved are under-recorded. Treat the war share as an upper bound on the prior, not a point estimate.

cases.name: Tribal lashkar invasion of Jammu and Kashmir

covert_infiltration_offensive.selection_note: Cases are offensives in Jammu and Kashmir that began with irregular or disguised forces crossing the ceasefire line or LoC with Pakistani state backing (1947 tribal lashkar, 1965 Operation Gibraltar, 1999 Kargil). The degree of state direction in 1947 is contested; in 1965 and 1999 regular Pakistani troops were involved. The set is complete for the major episodes and excludes the diffuse post-1989 infiltration of militants, which is a campaign rather than a discrete case. n=3 and only 1999 occurred under nuclear deterrence: use as history, not as a rate.
covert_infiltration_offensive.note: only 3 comparable cases: use as a rough prior, not a percentage

cases.name: Operation Meghdoot: India occupies the Siachen glacier

feature_seizure_clash.selection_note: Cases where control of a feature changed hands by force or by unopposed occupation (1974, 1988, 1995). Complete for PRC acquisitions of occupied or newly occupied Spratly/Paracel features that are well documented; omits the less-documented occupations of the 1970s-80s by Vietnam, the Philippines and Malaysia, so it over-represents PRC gains. n is tiny.
feature_seizure_clash.note: only 4 comparable cases: use as a rough prior, not a percentage

cases.name: Pulwama bombing and Balakot air strikes

militant_attack_retaliation_crisis.selection_note: Cases are India-Pakistan crises whose trigger was a mass-casualty militant attack in India that New Delhi attributed to Pakistan-based groups (2008 Mumbai, 2016 Pathankot, 2016 Uri, 2019 Pulwama, 2025 Pahalgam). The 2001 Parliament attack belongs here too but is filed as case:2001_parakram under border_mobilization; count it when asking how attack-triggered crises end. Pathankot is included deliberately as a no-retaliation case to offset the bias toward famous escalations, but many smaller attacks that produced no crisis are omitted, so the set measures how CRISES ended, not how often attacks cause one. All cases post-date the 1998 nuclear tests. 'limited_conflict' means cross-border kinetic action that stopped within days; 'de_escalation' means no military retaliation. Attribution of each attack is contested by Pakistan. The post-2016 cases show a trend (see tendency:india_escalating_retaliation), so weight recent cases above 2008.
militant_attack_retaliation_crisis.note: only 5 comparable cases: use as a rough prior, not a percentage

timeline.name: Coup against Prime Minister Mossadegh
timeline.line: US- and UK-backed coup removes Mossadegh after oil nationalization
timeline.description: After Iran nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, a CIA- and MI6-supported operation restored the Shah's authority. The CIA acknowledged its role in documents released in 2013.
timeline.immediate_effect: Shah consolidated power; oil consortium with Western majors.
timeline.long_term_effect: A documented grievance central to the Islamic Republic's narrative of foreign interference.

timeline.name: Iranian Revolution and embassy seizure
timeline.line: Revolution replaces the monarchy; US embassy seized in November
timeline.description: The Pahlavi monarchy fell in February 1979; the Islamic Republic was proclaimed in April; the US embassy was seized on 4 November and 52 hostages held for 444 days.
timeline.immediate_effect: Rupture of US-Iran relations that has never been repaired.
timeline.long_term_effect: Sanctions architecture, US regional basing and Iran's 'resistance' posture all descend from this break.

timeline.name: Carter Doctrine
timeline.line: US declares any attempt to control the Gulf an assault on its vital interests, to be repelled by force
timeline.description: Announced in the State of the Union after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iranian revolution. The basis for CENTCOM and the permanent US naval presence.
timeline.immediate_effect: Rapid Deployment Force created.
timeline.long_term_effect: Documented doctrine that still frames US responses to Hormuz threats.

timeline.name: Iran-Iraq War
timeline.line: Eight-year war with Iraq, including the Tanker War in the Gulf
timeline.description: Iraq invaded in September 1980; the war settled into attrition with chemical weapons use by Iraq and missile strikes on cities. Iran accepted UNSCR 598 in July 1988.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hundreds of thousands dead; no border change.
timeline.long_term_effect: Iran's missile program, self-reliance doctrine and distrust of international institutions (which did not condemn Iraq's chemical use forcefully) are commonly traced to this war.

timeline.name: Tanker War
timeline.line: Tanker War: hundreds of ships attacked; US reflags Kuwaiti tankers and destroys Iranian platforms
timeline.description: Iraq attacked Iranian tankers and Kharg Island; Iran retaliated against Gulf Arab shipping. The US reflagged Kuwaiti tankers (Operation Earnest Will, 1987) and, after USS Samuel B. Roberts hit a mine, destroyed Iranian oil platforms and naval units (Operation Praying Mantis, April 1988). USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air 655 in July 1988. The strait was never closed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran's conventional navy was badly damaged; Iran accepted a ceasefire weeks later.
timeline.long_term_effect: The origin of the IRGC Navy's asymmetric small-boat and mine doctrine, and of the US pattern of escorting shipping rather than striking Iran proper.

timeline.name: Closure threats during the 2011-12 sanctions escalation
timeline.line: Iran threatens to close the strait if oil sanctions bite; exercises follow; no closure
timeline.description: As the EU oil embargo and US financial sanctions were adopted, Iranian officials said not a drop of oil would pass; Iran held naval exercises and the US sent carriers. Traffic continued.
timeline.immediate_effect: Oil price premium; no interdiction.
timeline.long_term_effect: Established that closure threats are a bargaining signal that has not been executed.

timeline.name: Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action
timeline.line: JCPOA caps enrichment for sanctions relief; endorsed by UNSCR 2231
timeline.description: Iran accepted limits on enrichment and stockpiles with IAEA verification in exchange for lifting nuclear-related sanctions.
timeline.problem_solved: Iranian breakout time under a year.
timeline.did_it_survive: The US withdrew in May 2018; Iran exceeded the limits from 2019 and had enriched to 60 percent by 2021; the deal was moribund by 2025.

timeline.name: US withdraws from the JCPOA; 'maximum pressure'
timeline.line: US exits the deal and reimposes sanctions; the 2019 Gulf incidents follow within a year
timeline.description: The US reimposed and expanded sanctions, driving Iranian oil exports down sharply in 2019.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iranian economy contracted; Iran began exceeding JCPOA limits in 2019.
timeline.long_term_effect: The precedent Iranian negotiators cite for demanding guarantees against future US reversals.

timeline.name: 2019 tanker attacks, drone shoot-down and seizures
timeline.line: Limpet-mine attacks on tankers, an RQ-4 shot down, the Stena Impero seized; no closure
timeline.description: Attacks on tankers off Fujairah (May) and in the Gulf of Oman (June) attributed by the US to Iran; Iran shot down a US RQ-4 on 20 June and the US called off a retaliatory strike; the IRGC seized the British-flagged Stena Impero on 19 July after the UK detained an Iranian tanker at Gibraltar. Both ships were released by late September.
timeline.immediate_effect: Insurance premiums rose; coalition escort missions formed.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed Iran's preference for deniable, reversible actions against shipping and the US preference for avoiding direct strikes on Iran.

timeline.name: Attack on Saudi Abqaiq and Khurais facilities
timeline.line: Drone and missile strike halves Saudi output for days; Houthis claim it, US and Saudi Arabia blame Iran
timeline.description: The largest single disruption of oil supply in history by volume, for a short period. Attribution to Iranian territory was asserted by the US and Saudi Arabia; Iran denied it; the Houthis claimed it.
timeline.immediate_effect: Brief oil price spike; no US military response.
timeline.long_term_effect: Demonstrated that Gulf energy can be hit without touching the strait.

timeline.name: US strike kills Qasem Soleimani; Iran strikes Al Asad
timeline.line: US kills Soleimani; Iran fires missiles at US bases in Iraq with advance warning; both sides stop
timeline.description: Iran's 8 January ballistic-missile strike on Al Asad and Erbil was preceded by warning through Iraq; no US personnel were killed and the US did not respond. Iran then mistakenly shot down flight PS752.
timeline.immediate_effect: De-escalation within a week.
timeline.long_term_effect: The clearest documented case of Iranian retaliation calibrated to avoid war.

timeline.name: 2023 tanker seizures (Advantage Sweet, Niovi)
timeline.line: Iran seizes two tankers in a week; the US adds naval assets; traffic continues
timeline.description: Seizures followed US confiscation of Iranian oil cargoes under sanctions. The US announced additional F-35s, F-16s and a destroyer to the region in the following months.
timeline.immediate_effect: Tit-for-tat cargo seizures.
timeline.long_term_effect: Confirmed the seizure-for-seizure pattern.

timeline.name: First direct Iran-Israel strikes
timeline.line: Iran fires drones and missiles at Israel in April and October 2024; Israel strikes Iranian air defenses
timeline.description: After Israel struck Iran's consulate in Damascus on 1 April, Iran launched roughly 300 drones and missiles on 13-14 April, mostly intercepted with US and allied help; a second, larger ballistic strike followed on 1 October after the killing of Hezbollah's leader; Israel struck Iranian air defenses and missile production on 26 October.
timeline.immediate_effect: The shadow war became direct; the strait was not affected.
timeline.long_term_effect: Set the escalation ladder that the June 2025 war climbed.

timeline.name: June 2025 Israel-Iran war and Majlis closure vote
timeline.line: Israel and then the US strike Iran's nuclear sites; parliament votes to close Hormuz; the strait stays open and a ceasefire follows
timeline.description: Israel opened a campaign against Iranian nuclear and military targets on 13 June; the US struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan on 22 June; Iran's parliament voted the same day to close the strait, a decision left to the Supreme National Security Council and not executed; Iran fired a telegraphed salvo at Al Udeid on 23 June; a ceasefire took hold on 24 June.
timeline.immediate_effect: Twelve-day war; oil rose then fell back when the strait stayed open.
timeline.long_term_effect: Even under direct attack on its nuclear program, Iran did not close the strait; the strongest data point yet for the not_implemented pattern, and also a data point for how far escalation can go without closure.

lessons.name: US: Gulf access is a vital interest to be defended by force
lessons.description: Stated in the 1980 State of the Union and never rescinded; the institutional expression is CENTCOM and Fifth Fleet.

lessons.name: Iran: no outside power will protect it, so build missiles and asymmetric naval forces
lessons.description: Widely attributed by analysts to the Iran-Iraq War experience of missile attacks on cities and muted international response to chemical weapons. Iranian officials invoke the war constantly, so the linkage is well supported, but the doctrine is not laid out in a single public document.

lessons.name: Iran uses the strait as a threat it cannot afford to execute
lessons.description: Inference from the historical record (no closure in any crisis) and from Iran's export dependence on the same waterway. A regime facing existential defeat could still act against its economic interest; the inference weakens as Iran's stake in the strait's traffic falls.

tendencies.name: Iran retaliates in ways that are visible, deniable or telegraphed, and stop short of war with the US
contradicting: The 1984-88 Tanker War escalated to direct US-Iran naval combat; the 2019 Abqaiq attack, if Iranian, was a major unclaimed strike on a US partner; the October 2024 salvo was larger and less telegraphed than April's.
current_evidence: The June 2025 Al Udeid strike was announced in advance through Qatar and caused no casualties.
tendencies.caveat: Calibration has held while the regime's survival was not at stake. The June 2025 strikes on nuclear sites are the closest test so far, and the regime still calibrated; a leadership succession or an internal crisis could change the calculus.

path_dependencies.name: From 1979 to export dependence on China through the same strait

chain.step: 1979 revolution and hostage crisis break US-Iran relations
Sanctions regimes accumulate (1979, 1995, 2006-10 UN, 2012 EU, 2018 US)
Iran's oil exports narrow to a small set of buyers, mostly China, shipped through Hormuz
Current constraint: closing the strait would cut Iran's main revenue; threatening it remains cheap

path_dependencies.description: Documented sanctions and trade data; the constraint on Iranian behaviour is an assessment.

narratives.name: Iran: a century of foreign interference justifies resistance and self-reliance
narratives.modern_interpretation: The Islamic Republic frames its foreign policy as resistance to US and Israeli domination. The 1953 coup is documented; the claim that current US policy continues it is a political interpretation.

narratives.name: US: Iran as a hostage-taking, terror-sponsoring regime since 1979
narratives.modern_interpretation: Frames US policy across administrations and constrains any president's room to normalize relations. The events are documented; the framing is a domestic political narrative.

cases.name: Closure threats during the 2011-12 sanctions escalation
2019 tanker attacks, drone shoot-down and seizures
June 2025 Israel-Iran war and Majlis closure vote
Iran blocks Hormuz and imposes a permit-and-toll regime

hormuz_disruption.selection_note: Cases are episodes in which Iran threatened, attacked or seized shipping in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Outcome 'limited_conflict' means attacks or seizures occurred without closure; 'not_implemented' means a closure threat was not acted on. No case in the record involves an actual sustained closure, which is the base rate the analyst should start from and then update with Iran's present dependence on the strait for its own exports.
hormuz_disruption.note: only 6 comparable cases: use as a rough prior, not a percentage
